newsitem.title: USA: Republicans found business promises hard to keep.
newsitem.headline: Republicans found business promises hard to keep.

text.p: Democrats howled last year when newly powerful Republicans hustled business lobbyists into the back rooms of Congress to write legislation revamping federal health and environmental rules.
Now, as the first Republican Congress in 40 years comes to a close, it is business that is doing the complaining.

Compared to recent sessions of Congress the Republican pro- business record is notable, analysts say. Achievements include a broad telecommunications law, securities litigation reform and overhaul of the securities market, $33 billion in small business tax breaks over 10 years and a free-market farm act.

But compared to Republican promises to host a deregulatory bazaar, the final output falls short for a host of reasons -- overreaching, the lack of a needed 60 Republican votes to limit Senate debate and President Clinton's veto pen.
"They went in with a bang and went out with a whimper and that was especially true of their pro-business agenda," said Stephen Moore of the free-market CATO Institute.

In the end, business never got its regulatory rollback, lost a long-sought capital gains tax cut, could not overcome Clinton's veto of product liability reform and saw Congress pass a 90-cents-per-hour minimum wage increase and federal mandates for private health benefits.
"There weren't a lot of victories," said a lobbyist for a major American corporation. "The bottom line is it could have been a lot worse."

Main street business groups defended the session, with a U.S. Chamber of Commerce official calling it the "most pro-business, pro-economic growth Congress in decades." But when asked to assess the final output even small business, which may have come out best, expressed some disappointment.

"For small business we think it was a very productive Congress," said Dan Danner, a vice president of the National Federation of Independent Business. "If you compare it to what some people's expectations were, it may not have lived up."

It wasn't supposed to be that way. From the beginning cutting federal regulation and easing the tax burden on business were key elements of the Republican agenda. Small business worked actively to elect Republicans in 1994, angered by Clinton's failed plan for universal health insurance.

House Republicans rolled to a quick start in 1995, passing Speaker Newt Gingrich's Contract with America in the promised 100 days, including a capital gains tax cut, billions of dollars in other tax breaks and product liability reform.
Congressional leaders drafted a seven-year balanced budget and began work to revamp major environmental laws.

Republicans also worked with "Project Relief," a coalition of influential business lobbyists that spent thousands of hours and millions in campaign contributions trying to push through stringent new controls on government rulemaking.
Project Relief led to screams by Democrats, who have long consulted closely with labour groups, that business was being let into the back rooms to roll back health and safety laws.

But the gears jammed. Regulatory relief did not make it through the Senate, where Democrats used the threat of filibuster to delay bills, knowing Republicans did not have 60 votes to limit debate. Clinton vetoed product liability.
Faced with growing public concern about the environment Republicans began to splinter, unexpectedly killing a House plan to curtail enforcement of clean air and water laws.

Clinton vetoed the balanced budget, including major pro-business tax cuts. Two government shutdowns engineered by Republicans in an unsuccessful bid to force a budget deal with the White House were wildly unpopular with the voters.

"We've been more successful than we ever would have dreamed at the beginning of last year ... the breadth and audacity of their assault really galvanised people," said Peggy Taylor, legislative director for the AFL-CIO.

Labour gave $40 million to Democrats in the 1994 elections and $2 million to Republicans. Overall business PAC contributions were closely split between the parties, but business giving to Republicans stepped up after they won.
Charles DiBona, president of the American Petroleum Institute, which represents big oil companies, said the biggest disappointment was loss of regulatory reform.
"It was as if that whole process was an attempt to rape the environment," DiBona said. "We saw it as an attempt to rationalise the system."

There were major successes for business. Congress overrode Clinton's veto of the securities litigation bill and approved a law to phase down Depression-era farm subsidies. It ended a 23-year-old ban on Alaska oil exports and gave a tax break to oil drillers operating in deep waters in the U.S. Gulf.

Lawmakers passed the biggest rewrite of telecommunications laws in six decades, letting local and long-distance phone carriers, cable-television operators and other communications firms get into each other's business.
But many of businesses' wins this year came as part of compromise bills Republicans worked out with Democrats -- a decidedly mixed blessing.

Republicans resisted for months, but Congress passed a Democratic plan to raise the minimum wage to $5.15 an hour. Republicans sugared the pill for small business, adding about $20 billion in tax breaks like acclerated depreciation and pension reform.

Congress also passed a bill to help Americans keep health insurance if they changed jobs. Republicans sweetened the package by letting the self-employed gradually deduct 80 percent of insurance costs. But business lost its fight to add malpractice reform and small business insurance pooling.
In the final days, Congress required insurers to let new mothers stay in the hospital 48 hours and provide greater parity for mental health benefits, as small business fumed.
